Unable to stop Ansar Allah on the battlefield, Riyadh has reportedly resorted to attempts to orchestrate [terror attacks ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74806)in Yemen’s capital.
Armed Forces spokesman Yahya Saree announced late Friday that the military had “thwarted criminal attempts” by the Saudi enemy to stage attacks in Sanaa “bearing the hallmarks of ISIS.”
On Saturday, Yemen’s Foreign Ministry warned that Sanaa “possesses the legitimate right to respond to any Saudi Daeshi activity targeting its security and stability,” and would “take the necessary measures.”
The ministry stressed that the terror plots brought “back to memory what the Saudi regime did in the past in many countries of the region, foremost among them Yemen, Iraq, Syria and others” – a reference to the Saudi royal family’s sponsorship of Sunni Islamist jihadist groups -including al-Qaeda-linked forces in Iraq and Syria, and Al-Qaeda in [the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) in Yemen.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74031)
[The Houthis](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74798) did not disclose the specific tactical details or targets of the alleged Saudi intel-sponsored terrorist plots, nor details on the measures taken to dismantle enemy terror cells. But the plots and Sanaa’s warnings of a “response” may explain the notable uptick in Houthi missile attacks on Saudi cities, including the capital, [Riyadh](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74802), over the [past 24 hours.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74817)

events.text:
🇨🇳🌏 How China is expanding its military footprint across Africa
China is steadily increasing its ability to operate far beyond its borders, and Africa is becoming an increasingly important part of that effort, the SCMP says in its analytical piece.
The latest example came in Egypt, where six Chinese J-16 fighter jets took part in the Eagles of Civilization exercise, marking the aircraft’s first known deployment in Africa.
The deployment itself was a test of China’s long-range military logistics. The fighters travelled around 6,000 km to Egypt in roughly nine hours with aerial refueling, demonstrating the PLA’s ability to move and support a combat-capable air package thousands of kilometers from home.
The exercise also gave Chinese pilots a rare opportunity to train against French-made Rafale fighters operated by the Egyptian Air Force.
The drills covered:
🔶Long- and short-range air combat
🔶 Air-to-ground strikes
🔶 Suppression of enemy air defenses
🔶 Combat search and rescue
🔶 Integrated command and control
The exercise also allowed the PLA to test its preparedness in areas such as strategic lift, logistics, and global command — capabilities that become increasingly important when operating far from China.
China has spent decades building military ties across Africa, gradually expanding from officer training and defense exchanges to naval deployments, peacekeeping missions, anti-piracy operations, and joint exercises.
The PLA’s anti-piracy missions in the Gulf of Aden, which began in 2008, forced China to develop the ability to rotate crews, deliver supplies, maintain equipment, and sustain operations thousands of kilometers from home. In 2017, Beijing opened its first overseas military support base in Djibouti, providing a permanent logistics hub near one of the world’s key maritime routes.
More recently, Chinese naval deployments have included Type 054A frigates, Type 039A/041 submarines, and supporting vessels operating as increasingly sophisticated task groups. Analysts describe this broader process as part of China’s effort to develop and refine its “expeditionary capabilities” far from home.
The latest Egyptian exercise shows how this approach is expanding into the air domain as well. Training against Rafales gives Chinese pilots exposure to a Western-designed fighter while allowing Beijing to deepen military cooperation with one of Africa’s most capable armed forces.
🗣At the same time, African countries are not simply passive participants in this process because they try to “engage with China for their own security, training, and diplomatic reasons,” experts say.
China’s expanding military role in Africa now serves several interconnected purposes:
🔴 Testing long-range logistics and expeditionary capabilities
🔴 Expanding defense partnerships with African states
🔴 Protecting Chinese investments, citizens, and maritime routes
🔴 Building experience for military operations far from home
For China, Africa is becoming a place where partnerships translate into real-world military experience.

events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🇾🇪⚔️🇸🇦 Saudi Arabia Tried to Break Ansar Allah But Made It Stronger
Saudi Arabia entered Yemen in 2015 expecting its air force, money and local proxies to drive Ansar Allah from Sanaa. Eleven years later, the movement still holds the capital, has expanded along the Red Sea coast and is pushing Riyadh’s allies farther south.
Five Saudi-backed formations defending western Yemen shared a payroll and biometric identification system. They did not share integrated training, unified command or a joint operations room. When government forces withdrew from Hays, the front unraveled and Mocha was lost soon afterward.
The retreat exposed what years of Saudi patronage had produced: competing armed factions dependent on the same foreign sponsor but unable to operate as one army. Riyadh paid for manpower and weapons without creating a force capable of holding the territory.
Ansar Allah now controls much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including Mocha, Dhubab and Mayyun Island near Bab al-Mandab. It is also [pressing toward Marib](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/14/why-the-houthi-advance-towards-yemens-marib-taiz-matters), the Saudi-backed government’s last major northern stronghold and the center of important oil and gas production.
Losing Marib would deprive Riyadh’s allies of their remaining population and revenue base in the north. It would also give Ansar Allah a stronger position from which to pressure Shabwa and Hadhramawt and dictate the terms of any future settlement.
Saudi Arabia’s energy routes are becoming vulnerable at the same time. Drones launched from Iraq disabled the East-West pipeline, which carries oil to the Red Sea while bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. Ansar Allah also struck the Khamis Mushait airbase in southern Saudi Arabia.
Riyadh built that pipeline to escape dependence on one chokepoint. It now terminates beside another increasingly shaped by Yemen. Pressure around Hormuz, Bab al-Mandab and Saudi territory itself leaves the kingdom with fewer safe routes for projecting power or exporting oil.
Washington has provided intelligence and targeting support but has not opened another war to rescue the Saudi project. Turkey and Pakistan have also remained outside the fighting despite their defense ties with Riyadh. The kingdom accumulated partners, weapons and proxy formations without securing allies willing or able to reverse its defeat.
Saudi bombing, Israeli leadership strikes and the billion-dollar US Operation Rough Rider all failed to break Ansar Allah. The movement emerged with more territory and greater leverage over Saudi military bases, energy infrastructure and Red Sea shipping.
Riyadh launched its war to dictate Yemen’s political future. Eleven years later, Ansar Allah is setting the military balance and the price of Saudi Arabia’s exit.

🇨🇳🤔 Flub or ploy? F-35 parts diverted to China, feared lost
 
China’s military may have gotten its hands on top-secret F-35 parts after a trans-oceanic shipment from Australia to the US somehow wound up in Hong Kong instead.
The sensitive shipment reportedly consisted of unserviceable F-35 parts heading to one of Lockheed Martin’s subcontractors for repairs and refurbishment. The jet’s stealth cockpit canopy was the only component mentioned by name in reports.
Even if it’s broken or damaged, dissecting the canopy would enable Chinese defense engineers to find out the exact composition of the chemical coatings used in the canopy’s manufacture to improve the jet’s radar absorption capabilities.
But if China has intercepted the parts, its engineers should be weary. More than a decade since their adoption into the US military, F-35s continue to have an abysmal mission readiness rate as low as 25%. 
On top of that, the congressional Government Accountability Office projects that the US will spend over $2.1T – the equivalent of over six annual Chinese defense budgets combined, [on the F-35 program](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71048).
Besides, China’s indigenous next-gen [jet programs are](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72670) already flying circles around their US counterparts in range, speed, payload size and missile reach, and closing the gap on stealth and low-observability performance metrics.
Maybe the ‘lost’ F-35 parts were deliberately diverted to Hong Kong to get China to spend themselves into bankruptcy [trying to replicate a](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74787) terrible American design. Nice try, Pentagon Petey! 😏

events.text:
🇮🇱🇸🇦🇺🇸 Israel to demand ‘compensation’ for US F-35 sale to Saudis: Wait, how does that work?
Tel Aviv is reportedly feeling a bit kvetchy over the Pentagon’s plans to sell $24B worth of F-35 jets to Saudi Arabia, and intends to demand “[compensation” from Washington](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74726).
Although the deal has yet to be greenlit by Congress, and the Saudis aren’t expected to get their jets for at least another five years even if it’s approved, a source told Israeli media Israel is already drawing up a list of goodies it wants as recompence.
JPost says Israel could demand “participation in the development and production of classified weapons systems,” including “space-based weapons,” plus more US involvement in Israeli missile interceptor programs, the sale of bunker buster and advanced drone swarm weaponry, or even new US aid in financing the purchase of [additional F-15 and F-35 squadrons](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73715).
The 19fortyfive defense news website suspects “compensation” could even take the form of [Boeing’s sixth-gen F-47 fighter](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72670) (which at this point remains little more than a PowerPoint presentation).
It’s unclear whether the Saudis will even get their $506M apiece jets (5x the price the US military pays). The last time the US promised F-35s to a Gulf nation, the UAE, as a sweetener to join the Abraham Accords, the talks ended up petering out.
 
Also, let’s get this straight: the US, ostensibly a sovereign nation, sells its defense hardware to another country, and a third country can just come in and demand free stuff?
Yep, it’s exactly how it works. US lawmakers codified the concept of Israel’s ‘qualitative military edge’ into law in 2008. The law demands that however many hundreds of billions of dollars the Arab oil sheikdoms pour into the US economy and its MIC, Israel, which gets many of its US weapons for free, always takes first priority.
As for the Saudis’ F-35s, who knows, maybe five years from now they won’t need them, with the House of Saud toppled and replaced with a Houthi-aligned revolutionary state calling itself the United Arab Republic of Arabia.

events.text:
This little yellow submarine could help ensure Houthi dominance over their new Bab al-Mandab possessions
 
Ansar Allah’s speedboat island-hopping campaign has left them in total control over the narrow maritime chokepoint separating the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden (and by extension, Europe and Asia).
 
Holding on to these areas may prove difficult if the Saudis or their Epstein Coalition allies try to assault the mostly barren, volcanic [rock formations](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74718) – which provide virtually no natural cover.
 
But the Houthis have a secret weapon – the Al Qariah (lit. ‘Striking Calamity’) – a ~5.5M unmanned underwater loitering munition packed with up to 300 kg of explosives – enough to disable or even sink ships as large as a US missile destroyer or mega tanker.
 
The Al-Qariah made its public debut in late 2024, when the Houthis showed off its ability to target moving mock enemy warships.
 
The weapon bears superficial resemblance to the US Navy’s REMUS 600 surveillance and seafloor mapping drone, which Houthi combat divers captured intact off their coast in 2018, (the US Navy insisted it was performing an innocent “meteorological study” …in the middle of a warzone).
 
But while Al-Qariah has a similar general shape and black-and-yellow bee-style color scheme, that’s where the similarities end – with the Yemeni system featuring a different propeller configuration, control fins, nose cone, communications mast and electronic brain.
 
The autonomous torpedo’s range has not been publicized. Analysts suspect the system is guided primarily by inertial navigation using pre-programmed coordinates, with optical cameras linked to a retractable RF transmitter mast allowing terminal phase course corrections.
 
Terminal phase control may extend 10-30km, or 100km+ if it’s protracted via a nearby airborne data relay drone. The Houthis could even create a physical, fiberoptic wire-guided variant (which would make it jam-proof, but reduce firing range to 10-20km).
 
All this means that even if the Houthis’ enemies launched coordinated air, naval and amphibious assault operations to seize their islands, they may face a slog unlike anything the US Navy has experienced in its modern history trying to hold them.
 
At a minimum, the fighters’ ‘Striking Calamity’ drone threatens to turn Bab al-Mandab into a literal ‘Gate of Tears’ for its enemies.
